title: Apple’s HomeViews Stuck in Dusty Warehouses for a Year, Gizmodo Reveals】
body:
Apple’s much‑anticipated HomeView smart display has finally emerged from a year‑long storage backlog, but the delay has left the device feeling more like a relic than a breakthrough. The delay, insiders say, was largely caused by a cascade of setbacks in Siri’s next‑generation voice‑assistant platform, which forced Apple to pause the HomeView’s production line while engineers re‑engineered core software components. The result is a product that will hit shelves next month already looking dated against rival devices that have already embraced newer design cues and more advanced AI capabilities.

The HomeView, unveiled in a low‑key event last spring, was billed as Apple’s answer to the growing market for “hub‑centered” smart home devices. Its glossy, rounded frame and fabric‑wrapped speaker were meant to blend into living‑room décor while delivering a seamless interface for controlling lights, thermostats, and Apple‑centric services. However, the device’s launch timeline has been repeatedly pushed back, with internal memos revealing that the primary bottleneck was not hardware scarcity but software integration. Apple’s Siri team, tasked with delivering a more conversational and context‑aware assistant, missed critical milestones, prompting product managers to halt assembly lines until the voice engine could meet the promised performance standards.

Industry analysts note that Apple’s reliance on a single, monolithic voice‑assistant architecture has become a liability in an era where competitors are adopting modular AI stacks that can be updated independently of hardware. Google’s Nest Hub and Amazon’s Echo Show have both rolled out incremental software upgrades that keep older hardware relevant, whereas Apple’s approach ties the device’s core functionality to a tightly coupled Siri update cycle. This strategy has forced Apple to keep HomeView units in warehouses, effectively “dust‑collecting” them for months while the company scrambled to align its software roadmap with hardware production.

The delay has also exposed a broader tension within Apple’s product pipeline. Sources close to the company describe a “choking” effect, where Siri’s lagged progress forced other projects to be reprioritized, slowing the rollout of new features across the ecosystem. The HomeView’s design, while aesthetically consistent with Apple’s recent hardware language, now feels retrograde compared to the ultra‑thin, edge‑to‑edge displays that dominate the market. Competitors have already introduced devices with built‑in generative AI assistants capable of more natural dialogue, proactive suggestions, and third‑party skill integration—capabilities that HomeView’s current software stack struggles to match.

Despite the setbacks, Apple remains confident that the HomeView will still find a niche among its loyal base. The company plans to bundle the device with a suite of services, including Apple TV+, Apple Music, and HomeKit automations, positioning it as a premium hub for existing Apple users. Moreover, Apple’s upcoming “Siri 2.0” overhaul, slated for release later this year, promises deeper contextual understanding and tighter integration with the HomeKit ecosystem, potentially breathing new life into the HomeView’s functionality. Retail partners have been instructed to emphasize the device’s design elegance and ecosystem synergy in marketing materials, hoping to offset concerns about its relative age.

Looking ahead, the HomeView’s launch could serve as a litmus test for Apple’s ability to synchronize hardware and software development cycles in a fast‑moving AI landscape. If the refreshed Siri platform delivers the promised experience, the device may still carve out a profitable segment and reaffirm Apple’s commitment to a cohesive smart‑home strategy. Conversely, if the software falls short, the HomeView could become a cautionary example of how even the most polished hardware can be undermined by delayed AI integration. As the device finally rolls out of its warehouse confinement, the industry will be watching closely to see whether Apple can turn a year of dust‑laden inventory into a catalyst for a more agile, software‑first approach to future smart‑home products.
